overview: Burkina Faso's women's health landscape is driven mostly by government fee-exemption policy and donor and NGO programs rather than by a dense private femtech startup scene. Since 2016 the state has provided free maternal and child care, and in 2019-2020 it became one of the first Sub-Saharan countries to make family planning free, alongside a large self-injectable contraception (DMPA-SC) self-care rollout. A small but real innovation thread exists: UNFPA's IMMI menstrual-tracking watch pilot and the Ouagadougou startup Kairos, whose YouthShield tool was selected for UNICEF Femtech Ventures in 2026. Progress is fragile amid a humanitarian crisis that has displaced over 2 million people, most of them women and children, and disrupted roughly 40% of health facilities.

sections.heading: Latest major news
sections.narrative: Recent activity centers on international femtech backing for a local startup, WHO-supported gains in contraception, and ongoing scrutiny of the free-care policy.

items.text: Ouagadougou-based Kairos and its YouthShield reproductive-health misinformation tool selected among 11 startups for the first UNICEF Femtech Ventures cohort, backed by Sweden and Temasek Foundation.
Gender-responsive budgeting forum in Ouagadougou reviews the free-care policy for pregnant women and children under five as a central fiscal-equity issue.
Parliamentary monitoring mission across seven regions finds free maternal and child care remains globally effective in public facilities despite persistent stockout and reimbursement challenges.
National reporting credits the free family planning policy with a rising contraceptive uptake rate.

sections.heading: Policy & strategy
sections.narrative: Burkina Faso's core lever for women's health is user-fee abolition, layered with a national family planning plan and a self-care contraception strategy.

items.text: Nationwide free healthcare (gratuite) launched for pregnant and lactating women and children under five, covering deliveries, cesareans, postnatal care and cervical/breast cancer screening.
WHO-supported pilot to promote self-injectable DMPA-SC contraception begins in four health districts, later scaling to more than 75% of districts.
Burkina Faso becomes one of the first Sub-Saharan African countries to adopt a free family planning policy, expanded to the national user-fee exemption in 2020.
Ministry of Health launches the national budgeted family planning plan 2021-2025.

sections.heading: Latest ecosystem moves
sections.narrative: The femtech-adjacent ecosystem is thin and largely donor- and incubator-driven, anchored by menstrual-health pilots, reproductive-health information tools and a social-enterprise incubator.

items.text: UNFPA and UK femtech IMMI ran a menstrual-tracking watch pilot with ~300 adolescent girls in Burkina Faso and Moldova (June-November 2022); knowledge of period timing rose from 47% to 82%.
Kairos (Ouagadougou) develops YouthShield, a social-media monitoring tool that flags harmful reproductive-health misinformation for women and girls.
La Fabrique, West Africa's first social-enterprise incubator (founded 2014, Ouagadougou), supports impact startups including health-focused ventures.
WHO documents women's self-care gains via self-injected contraception, expanding access where providers are scarce.

sections.heading: Notable funding rounds
sections.narrative: There are no disclosed private venture rounds for Burkina Faso women's health startups; funding is catalytic and grant-based, led by UNICEF's equity-free program.

items.purpose: Scale a reproductive-health misinformation-detection tool for women and girls, plus a year of technical assistance.
Deploy app-free period-tracking watches to adolescent girls for menstrual-health education.

sections.heading: Key players & hubs
sections.narrative: The field is dominated by the health ministry, UN agencies and NGOs, with a couple of local startups and an incubator on the innovation side.

sections.heading: Active investors
sections.narrative: Capital reaching Burkina Faso women's health is donor and development finance, not domestic VC; regional gender-lens funds are active in West Africa but not documented in-country here.
